title: What if hashCode() always returns a constant?
shortTitle: What if hashCode() always returns a constant?
keyPoints: Legal but terrible for performance – all objects land in the same bucket
HashMap degrades from O(1) to O(n) because every lookup scans a single long chain
The contract is not broken (equal objects have equal hash codes), but distribution is destroyed
After Java 8, long chains become balanced trees (O(log n)), but still much slower than O(1)
A good hashCode distributes objects evenly across buckets

s1_definition.oneliner: It is legal but makes HashMap O(n) instead of O(1) because every object lands in the same bucket. A good hashCode distributes objects evenly.
s1_definition.profdef:
A constant hashCode:

- **Satisfies the contract.** Equal objects have equal hash codes (trivially, all objects do).
- **Destroys performance.** Every object goes to bucket 0. HashMap becomes a linked list.
- **O(1) → O(n).** Every get/put scans the entire chain. For 1 million entries, every lookup checks all 1 million.
s1_definition.analogy: Filing every bank account in the same drawer. Finding any account requires searching through the entire drawer instead of going directly to the right one.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  hashCode = constant:  all objects → one bucket → O(n) scan
  hashCode = well-distributed: objects spread evenly → O(1) average

  Java 8+: chain > 8 entries → tree → O(log n) worst case
  But O(log n) is still much worse than O(1)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A constant hashCode is legal but destroys HashMap performance. All objects land in one bucket, turning O(1) lookups into O(n) scans. A good hashCode distributes objects evenly across buckets.

One sentence to remember: a constant hashCode is legal but O(n) – a good hashCode distributes evenly for O(1).
